cues.text: Two Children on a Mountain Pasture
On the afternoon of September 19, 1846, two shepherd children from Corps in the French Alps were tending cattle above La Salette.
They were Mélanie Calvat , fourteen, and Maximin Giraud , eleven, who had met only the day before.
They saw a globe of brilliant light in a nearby hollow, as though, Maximin later said, the sun itself had fallen there.

Neither child had received more than the barest religious instruction, a detail later investigators weighed carefully when assessing whether the theological depth of the message the two would go on to report could plausibly have originated with the children themselves.
A Lady in Tears
As the light grew, the children made out the figure of a woman seated within it, her face buried in her hands, her shoulders shaking with what was unmistakably weeping.
She rose and spoke gently to them in French, urging them to come closer.
“Come, my children, do not be afraid, I am here to tell you great news.”
Throughout the long conversation that followed, tradition holds, the Lady wept continuously, even as she spoke.
A Message of Warning and Mercy
The weeping Lady spoke to the children of widespread neglect of Sunday worship and of blasphemy against her Son's name.
She also warned of a famine already beginning to spoil the region's wheat and potato crops—hardship of which the children were wholly ignorant and could not have invented themselves.
"If my people will not submit," she told them, "I shall be compelled to let fall the arm of my Son.
It is so strong and so heavy that I can no longer withhold it," language of a mother pleading for her children before a justice she herself could barely restrain.
She spoke too of a broken promise: farmers, she said, had once vowed to attend Mass in thanksgiving after a good harvest of potatoes.
They abandoned that promise once the crisis passed, and the crop failed again as a direct consequence—a specific, verifiable local detail neither child could easily have invented.
Secrets and a Shared Commission
Before departing, the Lady entrusted each child with a private message, spoken individually and kept from one another for years afterward.
She instructed both together with a final charge: "Well, my children, you will make this known to all my people."
She then withdrew up the mountain path, rose into the air, and vanished into the light.
By every account, the two children were transformed by what they had witnessed, even as they struggled to fully understand it.
Five Years of Careful Investigation

The local bishop, Philibert de Bruillard of Grenoble, opened a rigorous, multi-year inquiry into the children's testimony, the apparent authenticity of the crops' sudden restoration, and reports of healing associated with a spring that began flowing at the apparition site.
On September 19, 1851, exactly five years after the event, he formally declared the apparition worthy of belief.
Pope Pius IX and his successors have consistently upheld that judgment, even as the visionaries' later lives proved considerably more complicated.
Maximin's restless wandering and Mélanie's disputed later writings contrasted with the event that first brought them to public attention.
A curious sign accompanied the investigation: a stone broken from the site released a spring of water that had not flowed there before.
Reports of healing associated with that spring multiplied steadily throughout the years of the bishop's careful deliberation.
Legacy
A great basilica was built at the apparition site and consecrated in 1879, the same year Pope Leo XIII granted a canonical coronation to the venerated image of Our Lady of La Salette.

The shrine remains today a place of pilgrimage and of the Sacrament of Reconciliation in particular, fittingly, given the message of conversion first wept out over two frightened children on a lonely Alpine pasture.
Whatever weight later ages have given to the disputed private "secrets" the children carried, the Church's approved core of the apparition remains what it always was.
It is a mother's tears over sin and an urgent, tender plea for her children to return.
